power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objective: To describe global patterns of resting heart rate (RHR) in population subgroups and over time.

Methods: Observational data from WHO STEP surveys (n=363,462 participants from 76 countries, 2002-2020) and the South Asia Biobank (SAB, n=203,524 participants from four South Asian countries, 2018-2023).
RHR was measured in triplicate while seated using a blood pressure cuff.
Height and weight were measured using anthropometric techniques.
Physical activity was self-reported and accelerometry-measured (SAB subsample, n=22,183).
We describe RHR distributions by geographical region, temporality, sex, age, BMI, and physical activity.
Utility of RHR to explain accelerometer-based physical activity was examined by regression.
Results: Country-level median RHR ranged 65-80 bpm, higher in women than men.
Age-related RHR patterns diverged markedly by sex; men showing a curvilinear association with higher RHR in midlife, and women showing a consistent decline with age across most regions.
Compared to normal-weight, obese participants had higher RHR [WHO: (men: +4.4 bpm, women: +0.9 bpm, SAB: (men: +3.1 bpm, women: +1.0 bpm)].
Participants meeting physical activity recommendations had lower RHR [WHO: (men -1.6 bpm, women: -0.9 bpm), SAB: (men: -2.1 bpm, women: -0.5 bpm)] compared to insufficiently active.
In SAB (field-work spanning whole-calendar year), seasonal variations were present (0.6-0.9 bpm higher RHR in June-August compared to the Sept-Nov period), most pronounced further from the equator.
In 21 WHO countries with repeat survey data, RHR was stable over time in women but declined in men (-0.4 bpm/year).
Self-reported activity explained 2-14% (women: 2-3%, men: 10-14%) of the variance in device-measured physical activity, and RHR added 1-3% incrementally.
Conclusions: RHR varies globally, exhibits different age-related patterns by sex, and is higher in population subgroups with greater non-communicable disease burden.
RHR is easy to measure and may have utility for global health surveillance.

text.text: The gold-standard measurement of CRF is maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) during an incremental exercise test to exhaustion.
The feasibility of this assessment is, however, challenging in most situations, making it difficult to incorporate into surveillance systems.
Therefore, alternative methods are typically deployed, including heart rate response to submaximal exercise tests (13) but most cohort studies do not include dynamic exercise testing.

text.text: The most feasible indicator of CRF is resting heart rate (RHR) which is widely measured across national surveys, cohort studies and clinical settings; RHR has been shown to be inversely correlated with CRF (14).

text.text: To gain insights into the global variation of RHR and its potential for health surveillance, we describe the global epidemiology of RHR, with an enhanced emphasis on South Asia that has relatively high levels of NCDs.

Specifically, we integrate data from the WHO STEP surveys which collected RHR data from 76 countries globally, with the South Asia Biobank (SAB) which is a multicenter study focused on chronic diseases in four South Asian countries with additional objective measures of lung function and device-based physical activity (19, 20).
text.formatted: Specifically, we integrate data from the WHO STEP surveys which collected RHR data from 76 countries globally, with the South Asia Biobank (SAB) which is a multicenter study focused on chronic diseases in four South Asian countries with additional objective measures of lung function and device-based physical activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20)</ref>.

text.text: This dual-dataset approach provides a broad global overview while offering fine-grained insights into South Asia, allowing for comparisons of RHR levels between populations and assessing its potential utility for routine surveillance of cardiorespiratory health.
The WHO STEPS surveys, first administered in 2002, follow the WHO STEP-wise approach to noncommunicable disease risk factor surveillance (19).
text.formatted: The WHO STEPS surveys, first administered in 2002, follow the WHO STEP-wise approach to noncommunicable disease risk factor surveillance <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: This analysis includes data on representative samples of 363,462 individuals aged 18 and above from 76 countries (100 unique surveys) across 7 world regions.
In total, 21 countries conducted repeat surveys (Micronesia: four surveys; Benin: three, the remaining 19: two each).
Step 1 of the survey is questionnairebased and includes demographic variables and behavioral information on diet, physical activity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and disease status.
Step 2 focuses on physical measurements, including anthropometry, resting blood pressure and heart rate.
SAB is a large-scale multi-center cohort study investigating determinants of chronic diseases in South Asian populations (20).
text.formatted: SAB is a large-scale multi-center cohort study investigating determinants of chronic diseases in South Asian populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20)</ref>.

text.text: Between 2018 and 2023, the SAB study recruited 205,356 adults aged 18 years and above, from 564 surveillance sites across four countries or five test regions (Bangladesh, North India, South India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka).

At the baseline visit, participants attended local study assessment centers in the fasting state, for a single visit, during which they completed a structured assessment that was standardized across all settings.

Data include self-report (demographics, diet, physical activity, smoking, alcohol, disease status), physical measurements (anthropometry, RHR, blood pressure, lung function), and device-based physical activity measures (accelerometry) in a subsample.
RHR was measured as the pulse rate during seated rest when blood pressure was assessed using automated sphygmomanometers.
Measurements were performed in triplicate in Step 2 in WHO STEPS and during the baseline clinical visit in SAB.
Values below 30 bpm and above 150 bpm were discarded as invalid.
The minimum pulse rate across valid measures for each individual was used as RHR in the present analyses to reflect the most rested state.
We also conducted a sensitivity analysis using the median value.

RHR was described in different population subgroups: Sex (male, female), age group (18-24, 25-44, 45-64, 65+), BMI groups (underweight [<18.5, normal [18.5-24.9], overweight [25-29.9], obese[30+]), self-reported moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) as assessed by the global physical activity questionnaire (meeting/not meeting 150 min/week MVPA guideline), dietary intake (consume five or more servings of fruits and vegetables daily/ does not consume five or more servings of fruits and vegetables daily/ missing), smoking status (smoker/nonsmoker), alcohol status (drinker/non-drinker), marital status (single/married or cohabiting/divorced or separated/widowed), occupation (government/non-government employee/self-employed/ homemaker/unemployed/ Student/Retired/Non-paid/Missing), and education (no formal schooling, less than primary school completed, primary school completed, secondary school completed, college, postgraduate, missing).

text.text: Levels for some covariates (e.g., occupation and education) differed between datasets due to survey-specific categorisations but were harmonised for analysis where possible.

In WHO STEPS, countries were also aggregated into regions (Sub-Saharan Africa, Central and East Asia, East Europe and West Asia, Latin and South America, Middle East North Africa, Small Island Nations, South and Southeast Asia) to describe broader place variation.
Time (era) was parameterised as survey year centered on 2010.
Income was parameterised using countryspecific classification (low, lower-middle, upper-middle, high).
In SAB, test region (Pakistan, North India, South India, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh) was used to explore place differences.

Time was expressed as calendar year centered on 2021 (mid-survey year) to capture any secular trends over the short time span of this fieldwork, whereas seasonal variation within year was captured as month of year.
Personal income was parameterised in country-specific quartiles.
Prevalent metabolic disease status (yes/no) was concatenated from clinical interview questions of hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and type 2 diabetes.
Fat mass was derived from bioelectric impedance and expressed relative to height squared as fat mass index (FMI) to provide an alternative adiposity measure to BMI.

Physical activity was also measured objectively with a wrist-worn accelerometer in a subsample (n=22,183); MVPA was defined as wrist acceleration above 125 mg, aggregated in 5-sec analysis epochs and expressed as average weekly MVPA duration (min/week).
Lung function, another proxy indicator of cardiorespiratory fitness, was measured by spirometry.

Forced vital capacity (FVC) and forced expiratory volume (FEV1) were measured in triplicate, and the highest value across reproducible trials (within 0.15L of the second-best value) was retained per participant.
FEV/FVC ratio was derived from these and categorised as high (<0.5), medium (0.5 to 0.7), and low (>0.7) obstruction to distinguish levels of airflow obstruction (21).

text.text: SAB and WHO data were analysed separately.
Sex-stratified RHR percentiles (5 th , 25 th , 50 th , 75 th , 95 th ) were calculated and visualized using boxplots, violin plots, and line plots, stratified by population subgroup.
The association with age was modelled using cubic splines with three degrees of freedom, fitted as a three-way interaction with sex and world region.
In SAB, the same specification was applied but with test region to examine patterns between SAB test regions.
Place was examined by country and world region.
The BMI-RHR association was examined ecologically to assess if RHR may rank countries by this NCD risk factor.
To align WHO and SAB results, common analytical methods were applied where possible, with extensions for more detailed information in SAB.

To examine influence of survey approach, RHR distributions were compared in countries (Bangladesh and Sri Lanka) which had data from both WHO and SAB using medians (with percentiles), violin plots, boxplots, and Wilcoxon ranksum tests, stratified by sex, age group, and survey.
BMI was examined both categorically (underweight, normal, overweight, obese) within the multilevel models described below, and continuously.
For the continuous analysis, cubic splines were fitted separately within each sex, adjusting for country (WHO) or test region (SAB).
For SAB, additional associations of RHR with FMI, lung function categories and device-based physical activity tertiles were explored.
Potential regional heterogeneity in associations was explored by region-stratified analyses.

In WHO STEPS, population median RHR trends over time (survey year centered on 2010) were visualized via line plots in the 19 countries with repeat surveys; a subset regression model (countries with repeats) specifically assessed secular trends.

In SAB, seasonal variation in RHR was examined by test region using both cosinor models and time-of-year categories (Sept-Nov, Dec-Feb, Mar-May, June-Aug), with adjustment for calendar year (centered on 2021) to capture any short-term secular patterns.
We examined RHR patterns in relation to all above-considered explanatory variables in sexstratified regression models.

We used generalized linear multilevel models with a Gamma distribution and log link mutually adjusted for all explanatory variables, levels specified as individual and country to account for clustering by country.
In WHO, analyses were weighted by population size.
As SAB is a community-based study not necessarily designed for national representativeness, unweighted analyses were used.
In SAB, crude linear regression models evaluated RHR as a potential additional predictor of device-based physical activity, comparing models with GPAQ alone and RHR + GPAQ.
For completeness, we repeated this evaluation swapping GPAQ as the dependent variable and treating device-based MVPA as predictor.
Model performance was evaluated via R² values.

Analyses were stratified by sex and age group (18-44 and 45+ years) and additionally by country, to explore RHR's complementary value to self-reported or device-based physical activity measures in population subgroups.

This study integrates WHO STEPS surveys and the South Asia Biobank to describe global and regional distributions of RHR and evaluate its potential utility in non-communicable disease surveillance.
Age-related patterns diverged by sex, with RHR increasing and then declining with age in a curvilinear pattern in men across most regions, while in women RHR was steadily declining with age.
Higher BMI and insufficient physical activity were universally associated with elevated RHR.
Repeat cross-sectional survey results indicated long-term temporal stability with modest declines in men but seasonal variation was observed in non-equatorial regions.
RHR added to the prediction of device-based physical activity, over and above that of self-reported physical activity.
As RHR is already widely available in large population surveys and an easy-tomeasure vital sign, our results suggest RHR may have utility in routine global health surveillance.
In most regions, men exhibited a curvilinear age-RHR pattern, with higher RHR in midlife and lower values at older ages, whereas women showed a consistent decline.

The rise in RHR in men to a midlife peak followed by decline mirrors patterns in two large wearable cohorts, 92,457 Fitbit users in the US and 4.8 million Fitbit users geolocated across 217 countries and territories (22, 23).

text.text: RHR patterns in women are less consistent.
The US cohort showed a midlife peak while the global cohort showed a plateau or steady decline (22, 23).

text.text: Our findings extend these observations to population-based samples from low-and middle-income settings that are underrepresented in the literature.
The male curvilinear pattern likely reflects the competing physiological processes across the lifespan.

Age-related reductions in parasympathetic tone elevate RHR through midlife, while selective survival may produce an apparent decline in the oldest age groups, given the established association between elevated RHR and cardiovascular mortality (18, 24, 25).

text.text: These divergent patterns suggest that sex differences in RHR reflect differences in cardiovascular ageing which may have implications for potential reference standards.
Within SAB, the association between RHR and age varied substantially across test regions in men.
Only Sri Lankan men showed a monotonic decline but the relationship was inverse Ushaped in other countries.
Women across all test regions showed monotonic declines, consistent with the WHO regional findings.

As cardiometabolic disease patterns also vary across South Asia, in India for example diabetes prevalence ranges from 4.8% to 26.4% between states (27), healthy volunteer bias may also contribute to observed associations with varying response patterns in different test regions within SAB (20).

text.text: Taken together, these associations suggest that RHR captures meaningful biological information across diverse populations and measurement contexts.

text.text: With that said, studies observing RHR differences across the year are inconsistent.
Vukosavljević et al. found RHR to rise in unusually hot and cold temperatures while another study in Burkina Faso found no association between heat exposure and nocturnal heart rate (23, 29).

text.text: Irrespective of mechanism, an unbiased annual estimate of RHR requires repeat sampling across the year or statistical correction for season.

text.text: It is possible that differences in measurement protocols and participant selection across survey waves may partially explain this phenomenon (32, 33).

text.text: For example, participants in later survey years may be more or less rested than participants in earlier survey years due to different circumstances in the home where the measurement took place, and such biases over time could mask true changes in population RHR levels.

Confirming genuine secular trends in RHR requires standardized measurement conditions that do not yet exist uniformly across national surveys, and it could be debated if survey designs have captured the true resting state of participants and consistently so over time (14).
text.formatted: Confirming genuine secular trends in RHR requires standardized measurement conditions that do not yet exist uniformly across national surveys, and it could be debated if survey designs have captured the true resting state of participants and consistently so over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: Although RHR is relatively robust to routine stressors shifting by less than 2% after hard training, it rises by around 6% during illness (34).
text.formatted: Although RHR is relatively robust to routine stressors shifting by less than 2% after hard training, it rises by around 6% during illness <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(34)</ref>.

text.text: As personal wearables with continuous heart rate monitoring capabilities are becoming more common, such data could support our findings with more robust measurements of the true resting heart rate level, for example during sleep, which is also the estimate of RHR that correlates more closely with cardiorespiratory fitness levels (14).
text.formatted: As personal wearables with continuous heart rate monitoring capabilities are becoming more common, such data could support our findings with more robust measurements of the true resting heart rate level, for example during sleep, which is also the estimate of RHR that correlates more closely with cardiorespiratory fitness levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: The utility of RHR as a global surveillance tool relies on its accessibility and its biological validity.

RHR is routinely captured alongside blood pressure in surveys like WHO STEPS, requires no additional equipment or specialist training, and is feasible in low-resource settings where VO2max testing is not (14).
text.formatted: RHR is routinely captured alongside blood pressure in surveys like WHO STEPS, requires no additional equipment or specialist training, and is feasible in low-resource settings where VO2max testing is not <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: RHR is altered with physical training and is prospectively associated with health outcomes (18, 35).
text.formatted: RHR is altered with physical training and is prospectively associated with health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">35)</ref>.

text.text: Elevated RHR in high-risk regions, particularly in Pakistan where both RHR and adiposity were highest, underscores its utility.
These patterns identify subpopulations at elevated metabolic disease risk where NCD burden is high and fitness data are scarce (12, 36).
text.formatted: These patterns identify subpopulations at elevated metabolic disease risk where NCD burden is high and fitness data are scarce <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">36)</ref>.

text.text: We also demonstrate the complementary value of RHR to self-reported physical activity which further strengthens the case for its use in routine surveillance.
This was most evident in men.
Device-measured activity in women was found to be poorly explained by all examined predictors in our study.
This is possibly due to wrist-worn accelerometers detecting upper-body and domestic tasks that impose less sustained whole-body movement and cardiovascular load (37).

The growing affordability of commercial wearables that continuously measure both physical activity and heart rate opens additional opportunities for personalized CVD risk stratification and community-based screening (38,39).
Currently, however, most users are concentrated in highincome populations, with limited coverage in South Asia and Africa where NCD burden is high (23, 40).
text.formatted: Currently, however, most users are concentrated in highincome populations, with limited coverage in South Asia and Africa where NCD burden is high <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(23,</ref> <ref type="bibr">40)</ref>.

text.text: Whilst wearable ownership is steadily increasing, surveys such as WHO STEPS and SAB are feasible avenues for capturing objective health indicators in populations underrepresented in the field.
The strengths of this study include its large sample and global coverage.
The use of population weighting enhances generalizability.
Repeated cross-sectional surveys provides valuable insights into population-level time trends in RHR for routine health surveillance.
Limitations include the cross-sectional observational design that limits causal inference, and differences between measurement protocols that may introduce heterogeneity and impact comparability.
Studies using follow-up data and linkage to health outcomes in non-Western populations are needed to assert associations and strengthen causal interpretations.
• Cardiorespiratory fitness is strongly associated with CVD and mortality but remains understudied globally, particularly in non-Western populations.

• Resting heart rate is a feasible proxy indicator for cardiorespiratory fitness, routinely captured in national surveys, but its global epidemiology and surveillance potential have not been systematically described.

• Globally, RHR generally ranges between 65 and 80 bpm • Men and women show divergent age-related RHR trajectories, with a curvilinear pattern in men • Higher BMI, insufficient physical activity, and prevalent metabolic disease are consistently associated with elevated RHR • RHR can improve the prediction of objectively measured physical activity, over and above that of self-report • RHR offers a low-cost, accessible tool for fitness surveillance in low-resource settings.
• Sex-specific and region-specific RHR reference values may improve population-level risk stratification and inform targeted NCD interventions, particularly in South Asia.
